title: Test day four
hookLine: notice what you skip: every guest sends an excuse to the great supper, and the host fills the seats anyway
tomorrow: what part of the rule would you miss if it were gone?

cards: The invite says maybe, then: can't make it, so sorry. Jesus told a story about that. A man prepares a great supper and invites many.
When it's ready, he sends his servant: come, everything is ready.

"And they all with one consent began to make excuse. The first said unto him, I have bought a piece of ground, and I must needs go and see it: I pray thee have me excused." Another has new oxen to try out.
Another has just married. The servant comes back with nothing but apologies. Seat after seat, empty.

teach.h: BRING IN THE POOR AND THE BLIND.
teach.b: The host is angry, and then he changes the guest list. Go out quickly, he says, into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor, the maimed, the halt and the blind.
There's still room, the servant says. So go further, out to the highways and hedges, and bring them in, so my house may be filled. Here's the teaching.
Jesus tells this at a dinner, right after a guest says how blessed it will be to eat bread in the kingdom of God.
Christians read it as a picture of that kingdom: the table is ready now, and the host doesn't cancel the feast. He fills it with people nobody thought to invite.
The story ends on a hard line: none of those first invited, the host says, will taste his supper. Notice the excuses, too. None is wicked.

A field, oxen, a wedding: all good things, all reasonable, all a way of saying not now. And in the story, not now turns into not at all. That's test day four: notice what you skip, and the reason you give.
And here's the week, gathered. My season, named. Version one, from what was real.
Half, the core kept. Test week, begun. Easy, the plain river.
And skipped: an empty seat at a supper that's ready now.

how: Christians read the parable of the great supper (Luke 14:15-24) as a picture of the kingdom of God: a supper ready now, which even reasonable excuses turn down, and a table filled with the poor and the overlooked. In a test week, skipped lines and the reasons given are noted without blame.

o: noticing what you skip, and the excuse you give
the fourth day of a diet when cravings hit
a quiz on the first three days of a course

games.q: the great supper: tap the pairs.
p: made a great supper and invited many
bought a field: have me excused
brought in from the streets and lanes
so that my house may be filled

s: in the parable, the guests' excuses are wicked or shameful
a field, oxen, a wedding: ordinary, reasonable things. Still, saying not now meant missing the supper.
when the guests refused, the host filled his table with people nobody had invited
the poor, the maimed, the halt and the blind, from the streets and lanes, then the highways.

games.q: your friend skipped her evening walk all week, each time with a good reason. what would the parable have her notice?
o: the excuses themselves: like a field and oxen, good reasons can still mean not now.
that she's a bad person; the parable says every excuse is wicked.
nothing; skipping only matters if someone else is keeping score.
games.why: none of the guests' reasons is wicked; each is a way of saying not now, and they miss the supper. The host's table gets filled anyway.

practice: Close your eyes and walk back through the four days of your test. Find one line you skipped, and the reason you gave it, said plainly, without scolding yourself, the way you'd hear a friend's reason kindly.
Then rest in the stillness for the rest of the time: today's supper is still ready.

wordCard.voice: Test day four: notice what you skip, and the excuse that goes with it. In the parable, the supper is ready now, and the host fills every seat.
